title: Worry about the unexpected
hookLine: worry only about what cannot happen; this is the world's way, nothing stays (Salok M9 51, ang 1429)

lines: A WORRY LIST ON AN ENVELOPE.
MUCH OF IT IS NO SURPRISE.
cards: A worry list, scribbled on the back of an envelope. The car is making a noise. Dad's knees are worse.
The kids will leave home one day. Everyone on this list is getting older. Some of these are real problems.
But read the list again and something odd shows up: much of it is not a surprise at all. Bodies age. Things wear out.
People move on. Guru Tegh Bahadur has a two-line salok about exactly this list, and it has a twist in its first line.

teach.h: CHINTA: WORRY. ANHONEE: WHAT CAN'T HAPPEN.
teach.b: It's salok fifty-one, on Ang fourteen twenty-nine. It opens: chinta taa kee keejeeai, jo anhonee hoi. In paraphrase: worry about the thing that would be anhonee, the thing that cannot happen, the thing nobody expects.
Chinta is the everyday Punjabi word for worry, the one a grandmother uses when you're late home. Anhonee is the odd one: the not-happening, the impossible. So the line sounds backwards.
Worry only about what can't happen? The second line explains.

teach.h: THIS IS THE ROAD OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: Ihu maarag sansaar ko: this is the road of the world. Nanak, thir nahee koi: nothing stays, nobody stands still. Here's the turn.
Change is not the anhonee. Change is what the road does every day. Aging, loss, the end of a season: these are the road itself.

If something truly unexpected came along, maybe that would deserve worry. But the things we dread most are the things the world has always done. Worrying about them is like worrying that the sun will set.
Notice what the Guru doesn't say. He doesn't say nothing matters, or that you shouldn't care for your father's knees.

teach.h: CARE IS ONE THING; WORRY IS ANOTHER.
teach.b: Care is one thing; chinta is another. Care takes him to the doctor.
Chinta lies awake rehearsing a loss that hasn't come, as if fear could stop the road from being a road. And remember who's speaking.

These saloks are traditionally linked to the last part of Guru Tegh Bahadur's life, before his execution in Delhi. The calm in them isn't the calm of an easy life. It's calm that looked straight at the road.

how: Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks are read near the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teachers cite salok fifty-one as a word against needless worry.

o: care, the kind that takes Dad to the doctor
worry, best saved for what can't happen
a prayer said when a loved one is late

games.q: worry about the unexpected — tap the pairs.

s: the salok tells people to stop caring about those they love
it separates care, which acts, from chinta, which only rehearses loss.
the salok treats change as the road of the world itself
aging and loss are the road itself, not the surprise.
this salok is from Guru Nanak's Japji
it's salok fifty-one of Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks, on Ang 1429.

games.q: you're lying awake dreading that your parents are getting older. by salok fifty-one, what's the move?
o: do the care you can do, and set the chinta down.
games.why: aging is the road of the world, not the anhonee. the Guru leaves room for care; it's the sleepless rehearsal he questions.

practice: Let the list come up, and pick one worry that's really about something the world always does: getting older, a child growing up, a season ending.

Ask whether there's one thing you can actually do; if there is, note it for later, and if there isn't, breathe out and set it down like a heavy bag on the floor. If you pray, say Waheguru as you let it go.

wordCard.voice: Chinta, worry. Chinta for the anhonee: save it for what can't happen, because change is the road itself.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: chinta, worry; the everyday Punjabi word, and the first word of salok fifty-one.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing stays. Care does what it can; chinta only rehearses. Day six hundred two, done.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, salok 51 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429)
